title: Something Has Changed...I'm Old Now
subtitle: Reflections on getting older.
body_html:
Getting older a grim business. Welcome to the Frontier Psychiatrists— it's a health- themed newsletter. I'm Owen Muir, and I'm a child adolescent and adult psychiatrist. I'm also at that age where I forget what age I am. I'm pretty sure it's 45. Oh, my. 45 years old… I'm slightly north of a midlife crisis, maybe. Some people get to it by this point in time, I hear. I have an autoimmune disorder. When I was younger, and had a lot of energy, which I don't at all anymore, I worried that having bipolar disorder was The Real Problem for me. The amount of time people with mood disorders, like mine, spend worrying about how that mood disorder limit their life is, in retrospect, adorable. It was cute to think that bipolar disorder would be the thing that limited me. I've written about this before, but end of the story? It is not even a real problem.

Ironically, it's not the real problem for almost anybody. Anyone who survives it will have other, more serious problems. The wolf in sheep's clothing? It's time itself. When you get older, you know what it was like to be young. You can remember what it was like to have a spring in your step. That magical time, in everyone's life, before they have an ankle injury. Before they have plantar fasciitis. Before they have aches. Before they have pains. When running down the street is something you do for fun, not something you do because you desperately need to or something terrible will happen. Running— just out of sheer glee—is something my children do, regularly, and I don't. Not anymore. Because… I'm getting old.

Being old means you're slower. It also means that young people, you know, those people around you, the people in their 20s, 30s, even early 40s, especially those who don't have chronic auto immune disease diseases? Those people don't seem to have the same slowness. But they will, and you know that. Because you've seen the future. You've seen the future by getting old yourself. It's absolutely the worst crystal ball you could hope for. I’ve looked in that Palintir. I look like Pippen on the other side of that experience. Or was it Mary?

At a certain point in your life, it becomes clearer that to other people, you're old also. My children are nine, almost. I'm definitely ancient to them. When I'm out in a social circumstance, I am aware that I am not mistakable as young anymore. I am balding. The top of my head is not covered with hair. Although some men go bald when they're younger, it's much more common when you're older, like I definitely am. Everyone can tell. One look, and the jig up.

I'm not exactly on the dating scene, but if I was, it's obvious I would be too old for people who didn't want an older partner. Now, for men, that's relatively normative in our culture. This getting older game is not exactly kinder to women than men. And it doesn't exactly apply to me, thank goodness. There are many people in my age bracket who are dating. There, but for the grace of God, go I.

You can't help but notice that celebrities are overwhelmingly young. The ones you recall as young and attractive? Some of them are dead. Carrie Fisher in Star Wars? What a knockout! The stuff of fantasies.

She is no longer alive.

You know how I write about obesity, and metabolic syndrome, and other side effects of psychiatric treatment leading to early death? According to Carrie Fisher, that's what happened to her. It's a huge bummer. I remember when she was young, and beautiful, and alive, and that's not the case anymore. I'm still here, the celebrities of my youth? Less and less so. I don't recognize these “popular characters” anymore, because we lionize the young, and thus we have to find new ones all the time, and some of those are going to be so new that I have no idea who they are. Young people will know, though, further solidifying the fact that I'm not one of them anymore.

This doesn't slow down, it doesn't go better, you never get younger. And that becomes obvious to you at a certain point in time. This is the stuff that middle-age crisis moments are made of. Soon, all of my friends will also be old—the best we can ask is to grow old gracefully.

I talked to my mom about it, who is in her 80s, and it definitely doesn't get better, or easier. When you get to be definitively old, not just contemplating being old, not only are your friends older, but many of them were dead. The people you loved? They are the people you lose. It's never a good day when you find out your friend has had a medical thing happen. Most things that happened to you when you're older, medically, are bad.

There are no more truly elective surgeries. There's only stuff that doesn't kill you yet. It's grim business. And that is why we have each other, to learn from, and accept the what comes. Apparently, as some point, there is wisdom to be had.
